title: Inuit & Sami Peoples
keyIdea: People have lived in the Arctic for thousands of years. The Inuit live in Alaska, northern Canada and Greenland. The Sami live in Sápmi, the far north of Norway, Sweden and Finland. They know the land, ice and animals very well. Inuit travelled by dog sled and kayak, wore caribou and seal skin, and built snow houses on winter trips. Many Sami herded reindeer. Both peoples live in the Arctic today and still speak their own languages.
familyTip: Find the Arctic on a globe: the top, around the North Pole. Point to Alaska, Canada and Greenland (Inuit lands) and to the north of Norway, Sweden and Finland (Sami lands). Ask your child: what would you wear at minus 30? Why does a snow house have a low tunnel? Then look up a few words in Inuktitut or Northern Sami together.

lab.caption: Flagship lab: tap the Inuit and Sami homelands, choose how to travel, use every part of a seal, dress for −30 °C, build a snow house and bust myths.

kid: The Arctic is the cold land and sea around the North Pole. People have lived there for thousands of years. The Inuit live in Alaska, northern Canada and Greenland. The Sami live in the far north of Norway, Sweden and Finland. They call their land Sápmi.

There were no roads on the ice. Inuit dogs pulled sleds over the snow and sea ice. In summer, hunters paddled a kayak, a thin boat made of seal skin on a wood frame. Many Sami families moved with their reindeer, and reindeer pulled their sleds. In winter the reindeer dug through the snow to eat lichen.

Inuit wore two caribou coats, called parkas. The fur of one faced in and the fur of the other faced out. Warm air was trapped between them. Seal skin boots kept their feet dry. On winter trips, hunters built a snow house from blocks of hard snow. The door was a low tunnel, so the cold air sank into it.

Arctic peoples took care of the animals they lived on. After a seal hunt, almost every part was used. The meat was food. The fat was burned in a stone lamp for light and heat. The skin made boots, and the bones made needles. Today Inuit and Sami live in towns and on the land. Many use phones and snowmobiles, and they still speak their own languages.
adult: Ages 7 to 9. Children should name the Inuit (Alaska, Arctic Canada, Greenland) and the Sami (north of Norway, Sweden and Finland) as Indigenous Arctic peoples. They should describe at least three parts of traditional life. They should also explain that this knowledge of the land built up over thousands of years. It fits well with work on polar regions and how living things cope with cold.

Key facts. The Inuit Circumpolar Council speaks for about 180,000 Inuit in Alaska, Canada, Greenland and the far east of Russia. Sápmi also reaches Russia's Kola Peninsula. Inuit tools include the qamutik (dog sled) and the qajaq (kayak), made of skin over a wood or bone frame. The qulliq is a stone lamp that burns seal oil. Winter clothes were two layers of caribou skin, with sealskin boots called kamiit. Snow houses were mostly winter travel and hunting shelters, used most in the central Canadian Arctic. In summer people lived in skin tents, and other homes were built of stone, turf and whalebone. Sami reindeer herding goes on today. Herders follow the herd between winter lichen grounds and summer pastures.

Common mistakes to watch for. Many children think Arctic peoples lived only in igloos all year, or that they belong to the past. Others mix up the Arctic (north, home to people) with Antarctica (south, no Indigenous people). Avoid the word Eskimo: many Inuit, mostly in Canada and Greenland, find it rude. The old name Lapps for the Sami is rude too. Be careful not to treat all Arctic peoples as one group: Inuit and Sami have different languages, histories and ways of life.

choices: The north of Norway, Sweden and Finland
practice.hint: Think of the lands on the far left of the Arctic map, plus the big island Greenland.
practice.explain: Inuit live in Alaska, northern Canada and Greenland. The Sami live in the north of Norway, Sweden and Finland.

practice.prompt: A dog team has {r} pairs of dogs pulling a sled. How many dogs is that?
practice.hint: A pair is 2 dogs. Count in twos, once for each pair.
practice.explain: {r} pairs × 2 = {=r*2} dogs. A dog team can pull a heavy sled over sea ice for hours.

practice.prompt: Why did Inuit wear two caribou parkas in winter?
choices: Two fur layers trap warm air
One coat was too heavy to wear
practice.hint: Think about what gets trapped between the two layers of fur.
practice.explain: Warm air is trapped between the inner parka (fur in) and the outer parka (fur out). That keeps the body warm at −30 °C.

practice.prompt: A Sami herd has {a} reindeer. In spring, {b} calves are born. How many reindeer are in the herd now?
practice.hint: Add the new calves to the reindeer already in the herd.
practice.explain: {a} + {b} = {=a+b} reindeer. Reindeer calves are born in late spring, when the snow starts to melt.

practice.prompt: Which way of travelling is best for creeping up on a seal in open summer water?
practice.hint: In summer the sea ice melts, so you need something that floats.
practice.explain: A kayak is light and silent, so a hunter can paddle close to a seal without a splash.

pool.prompt: What do the Sami call their homeland?
pool.hint: It spreads across the north of Norway, Sweden and Finland.
pool.explain: The Sami call their land Sápmi. It reaches across the north of Norway, Sweden, Finland and part of Russia.

pool.prompt: Why is the door of a snow house a low tunnel?
choices: Cold air sinks into the tunnel
So warm air can rise out
pool.hint: Warm air rises and cold air sinks.
pool.explain: Cold air sinks and stays low in the tunnel. Warm air rises and stays up by the sleeping bench.

pool.prompt: What was seal blubber (fat) used for?
choices: Oil to burn in a stone lamp
pool.hint: Think about how a family got light and heat in a dark winter.
pool.explain: Blubber was burned in a stone lamp called a qulliq for light, heat and cooking.

pool.prompt: A snow house has {r} rings of snow blocks. Each ring has {b} blocks. How many blocks is that?
pool.hint: Multiply the number of rings by the blocks in each ring.
pool.explain: {r} × {b} = {=r*b} blocks. Real rings get smaller near the top, so this is a quick estimate.

pool.prompt: What do reindeer eat in winter?
choices: Lichen dug out from under the snow
pool.hint: Reindeer use their hooves to dig through the snow.
pool.explain: In winter reindeer dig through the snow to find lichen. Sami herders move the herd to where the lichen is good.

choices: Inuit and Sami live in the Arctic today
Inuit and Sami only lived long ago
Inuit lived in igloos all year round
pool.hint: Think about the true or not true cards in the lab.
pool.explain: Inuit and Sami live in the Arctic today. Snow houses were for winter trips, not for the whole year.

pool.prompt: Why were seal skin boots good in the Arctic?
choices: They were very thin and light
pool.hint: Wet feet freeze fast in the cold.
pool.explain: Seal skin is waterproof, so the boots, called kamiit, kept feet dry and warm.

pool.prompt: How do young Inuit learn which sea ice is safe?
choices: Elders teach them over many years
Nobody knows which ice is safe
pool.hint: This knowledge was built up over thousands of years.
pool.explain: Elders pass down how to read the ice, the weather and the animals. That knowledge took thousands of years to build.

pool.prompt: A Sami herder moves the reindeer {a} km on Monday and {b} km on Tuesday. How far did the herd move in all?
pool.hint: Add the distance for Monday and the distance for Tuesday.
pool.explain: {a} + {b} = {=a+b} km. Herders walk with the herd between winter lichen grounds and summer pastures.
